How each format is grounded, for real this time

ArtifactParsed bySelector derived from
Declarations PDFpdf.js getTextContent() + Util.transform Text-item transform matrix composed with the viewport transform, normalised to percent of page box. The quote is matched against extracted text, then the item boxes it spans are unioned.
Endorsement DOCXfflate → word/document.xml → DOMParser Real w:p index and character offset inside the concatenated w:t runs. The XPath is the OOXML path, not a rendered-HTML path.
SOV XLSXfflate → xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml Actual r="E2" cell references read from the sheet XML. Column is resolved by header text, row by the Loc # key — not by position.
Loss run CSVNative text decode indexOf on the decoded string, offsets in UTF-16 code units then converted to code points.

Embedded snapshot versus your file

The four documents ship inside this HTML as base64 so the page runs with no network and no file picker. They are real byte streams — a genuine PDF, genuine OOXML zips, a genuine CSV — but they are a copy frozen at build time. Editing the standalone files next to this page has no effect on it, which is the correct behaviour for a self-contained artifact and a poor way to test anything. Load your own file instead: the badge in the toolbar switches from embedded sample to your file, the parse counts update, and the field anchors re-resolve against whatever you handed it. Most of the predefined fields will go unresolved against a document they were not written for — that is the honest result, and the anchor probe is there so you can point at real text in your own file and see the locator it produces.

What this actually proved, and what it didn't

Proved: the selector crosswalk survives real parser output. The PDF percentages come out of the transform matrix rather than a designer's eye, the DOCX offsets index real runs, and the cell references are the ones the spreadsheet itself carries. Anchoring by quote works, and when it fails the panel says so instead of pointing at the wrong place.

Not proved, and worth being blunt about it. These are clean, generated documents. A real submission package brings scanned faxes with no text layer, rotated pages, tables that continue across page breaks, merged cells, header rows that are not row 1, and DOCX produced by a broker's 2009 template with tracked changes still in it. The original_width/rotation handling and the OCR path are not exercised here at all. Treat this as evidence that the design is sound, not that the implementation is done.

The XLSX header assumption is the first thing that will break. This build resolves a column by matching header text in row 1. Real SOVs from brokers routinely have two or three banner rows above the header, merged title cells, or a second header block halfway down for a different location group. Resolve the header row explicitly during ingestion and store it in the locator rather than assuming row 1 — the panel already carries headerRow in the selector for exactly this reason.

On the PDF quote anchor. reportlab writes each line as a single text item, so quotes resolve to one item cleanly. Real PDFs fragment text far more aggressively — a single visual line can arrive as a dozen items split mid-word, and some producers emit them out of reading order. The multi-item union path in this build handles the simple fragmentation case; reading-order reconstruction is a separate problem that Docling solves server-side, which is the argument for anchoring against Docling's normalised text rather than pdf.js's raw items in production.

Documents are synthetic — carrier, insured, values and losses are invented — but the files themselves are real PDF, OOXML and CSV byte streams, embedded and parsed in the browser. pdf.js (Apache-2.0) and fflate (MIT) are bundled inline; nothing is fetched from the network.
